newsitem.title: USA: Trouble ahead for stocks if small firms break pattern?.
newsitem.headline: Trouble ahead for stocks if small firms break pattern?.

text.p: More than midway through what is usually one of their strongest months, small listed companies show few signs that their normal seasonal rally is at hand -- a fact analysts say bodes ill for the entire stock market.
The start of the New Year traditionally finds the market flush with retirement account cash. This year, that money has fuelled the Dow Jones industrial average's relentless run towards 7,000.
In late trading Monday, the 30-stock blue-chip index was up 7.31 points at 6,840.41, putting it above Friday's record close of 6,833.10.

But many experts are uneasy, and they see possible trouble ahead for the entire stock market, as the Russell 2000 index -- a barometer of the performance of small companies -- labours to overcome last July's sell-off.

Wall Street's willingness to embrace small capitalisation stocks is viewed as an important barometer of investor confidence. For now, the stock traders' buying interest rests firmly with big-name, highly-liquid issues.
Analysts believe that what happens to the Russell index in the next few weeks is critical.
Market capitalisation -- the total value of a company's outstanding shares -- runs from real estate investment trust Saul Centres Inc.'s $162 million to FirstMerit Corp., a bank, at $1 billion.
In contrast, General Electric Co., is the largest U.S. firm, with a capitalisation of $138 billion.
The experts say there are two reasons why small-name stocks must now assert themselves.

One is the "January effect," which refers to the time of year when the stocks of small companies rally as fund managers, flush with retirement account cash, pick up low-priced bargains created by December tax-loss selling.
Instead, buying has been concentrated on the big-name companies, such as International Business Machines Corp. and Intel Corp., which could be an ill omen.

"A handful of primary technology and big cap stocks, even in the OTC market, have been driving the indexes," said Ricky Harrington, technical analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane. "We really haven't seen a big push in small caps so we are not getting that real January effect."
"We should know by the middle of next month," he said. "If (small cap stocks) don't pick up by then, we could be hitting a correction."
The second reason is that the Russell 2000 index has just recently edged to record territory, some eight months after its last reached a high.
The index was particularly hard hit in July, dropping nearly 15 percent from its May highs.

It was not until Jan. 7 that the index recouped its losses and by last Friday's close, the Russell stood at 367.88, for a paltry 1 percent gain in eight months. In late trading Monday, the index was up 1.43 points at 369.31.
In contrast, the Dow industrial index was back in record territory by September, staged a furious rally in November and added 6 percent in new gains since the year started.
Analysts said the market was now at a major crossroads, and what happens to the Russell in the next few weeks was critical.

"The Russell has been underperforming since the end of December," said Peter Green, vice president of technical research at Gruntal & Co. "If it doesn't follow through on this rally, a lot of people will be disappointed, sensing this will be last phase of this bull market."
